summary: A 1970 set of notes from Steve Crocker on the protocol, following RFC 33. It updates RFC 33, and was in turn commented on and updated by RFC 39 and RFC 44. It is a working document from the early protocol design effort.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 36 adds notes to the early rules for how computers talk on the ARPANET, describing how to link their mailboxes, how to pause and resume when one is sending too fast, and how to reroute links between mailboxes.

questions: what are the arpanet host host control commands
how did early arpanet flow control work
what does the rsm command do
subtitle: Crocker's 1970 notes refining RFC 33, covering connection setup, flow control, and reconnection for early ARPANET host-to-host communication.

tldr.problem: The early host-to-host protocol needed a way to establish connections, to stop a sender from flooding a receiver, and to switch connections between sockets.
tldr.mechanism: Connections are established by exchanging RFC commands between sockets (a send/receive pair). Flow control uses modified RFNMs to pause and the RSM command to resume. Reconnection uses commands such as FND, END, RDY and ASG to chain connections between sockets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 36 updates RFC 33 and was updated by RFC 39 and RFC 44. The author notes the reconnection scheme was presented separately because of its complexity and limited experience with it.

today: RFC 36 is a working note (status Unknown). It updates RFC 33 and was updated by RFC 39 and RFC 44.

sections.title: Three Facilities
sections.content:
RFC 36 identifies three facilities: connection establishment, flow control, and reconnection. Reconnection is treated separately because of its complexity and because the author had limited experience with the protocol at the time.

Connection establishment is similar to RFC 33 but simplified (switching is handled separately). Roughly, each process grabs a socket and requests a connection to the other; each NCP sends an RFC command. The connection is established when each NCP has received an RFC and the RFNM for the one it sent. The two sockets must form a send/receive pair.
sections.plainLanguage: Two processes each pick a mailbox and ask helpers to link them. They are connected once both helpers have heard back from each other. The mailboxes must be a matching send and receive pair.

sections.title: Flow Control
sections.content:
To prevent a sender from flooding a receiver, the protocol allows the receiver to stop flow. When the receiver wants to inhibit flow on a link, it requests its IMP to modify the next RFNM on that link. The sending host interprets this as an RFNM and as a request to stop sending, and returns a confirming control command.

When the receiver is ready again, it sends an RSM command telling the sender to resume. The text notes a philosophical difference (BB&N argued for unlimited buffering) but the design assumes only small buffers on the receive end.
sections.plainLanguage: If the receiver is getting too much data too fast, it can tell the sender to pause. When it is ready again, it tells the sender to start up again.

sections.title: Reconnection
sections.content:
RFC 36 describes a dynamic reconnection scheme that allows switching one or both ends of a connection from one socket to another, even after flow has started. The author claims this provides generality (all forms of switching) and introduces no overhead on data messages (cost is borne in protocol processing).

The scheme uses control commands including FND (final end), END (end found), RDY (ready), and ASG (assign new link) to establish and complete reconnections. If a short-circuit within the same process is attempted, the chain may close on detection of a loop.
sections.plainLanguage: You can reroute a connection from one mailbox to another while things are happening. Special commands help track the chain and safely complete the switch.
